assignments.title: Reading Topographic Maps in 3D
assignments.subtitle: Relate contour lines to three-dimensional landscape form using Visible Geology
assignments.description: Using the Visible Geology Geology Explorer, build a layered geological block with valley topography and explore how elevation contours on a 2D map correspond to the 3D surface beneath them. Create six horizontal rock units using the Layers tool (Conglomerate 35 m, Sandstone 20 m, Siltstone 10 m, Shale 20 m, Limestone 25 m, Dolomite 35 m), then apply a Valley topography (Topography tool → Valley → View Contours on). Toggle between 2D map view and 3D block view to observe how horizontal beds and contours interact. This assignment also serves as your introduction to the Visible Geology interface — no prior experience required.
learningGoals: Navigate the Visible Geology Geology Explorer (rotate, pan, switch 2D/3D views, use Layers and Topography tools)
Explain why horizontal rock layers produce map contacts that parallel topographic contour lines
Identify the stream location and downstream flow direction from a contour map
Use correct topographic terminology: contour interval, ridge, valley, spur, col

deliverables.label: Annotated screenshots (2D and 3D views)
deliverables.description: Two screenshots of your finished block: one in top-down 2D map view and one in oblique 3D view. On the 2D screenshot, draw a line along the valley floor marking the stream location and add an arrow indicating downstream flow direction. Label at least one ridge and one valley in each view.

deliverables.label: Contour–contact relationship explanation (150–200 words)
deliverables.description: Explain geometrically why horizontal rock beds produce contacts that match topographic contour lines in the 2D map view. Include a description of what you observe as the contacts cross the valley and why they form a V shape pointing upstream.

deliverables.label: Practical application note (100–150 words)
deliverables.description: Describe how you would use a topographic map to plan a safe hiking route across hilly terrain or to assess slope hazard for a proposed infrastructure project. Reference at least two specific contour features (e.g., closely spaced contours, V-shapes pointing upstream).

criteria.label: Screenshots and annotations
criteria.description: Both 2D and 3D views captured; stream, flow direction, ridge, and valley correctly annotated.

criteria.label: Contour–contact explanation
criteria.description: Accurately explains the geometric reason horizontal beds parallel contours; V-shape in valley correctly described.

criteria.label: Practical application
criteria.description: Application to route planning or hazard assessment is specific and references named contour features.

assignments.attribution: Exercise design inspired by Abbey, A.L. (California State University, Long Beach). Hosted using Visible Geology (visiblegeology.com, Seequent Ltd.).

assignments.title: Dip Angle and Map Patterns
assignments.subtitle: How the angle of dip controls V-patterns and outcrop band width in a valley
assignments.description: Using a pre-built valley topography in Visible Geology, systematically tilt the six horizontal beds from the previous assignment and observe how dip angle changes the shape and orientation of outcrop bands in map view. Open the embedded model below (it loads a valley topography with horizontal beds). Use the Events tool → Tilt to apply each scenario; delete the previous Tilt event from the History panel before adding a new one so tilts do not compound. Test: upstream dip at 20° (Strike 0°, Dip 20° RHR), upstream dip at 60° (Strike 0°, Dip 60°), and vertical bedding (Dip 90°). Screenshot the 2D map view after each change.
learningGoals: Use the Visible Geology Events tool to apply Tilt events with specified strike and dip (RHR azimuthal notation)
Describe how dip angle controls outcrop band width and the sharpness of V-patterns in a valley
Explain why vertical beds produce contacts that are independent of topography
Predict the outcrop pattern for a given dip angle and dip direction relative to a valley

deliverables.label: Screenshot set — three dip scenarios
deliverables.description: For each of the three dip scenarios (upstream 20°, upstream 60°, vertical 90°) provide a 2D map-view screenshot with the tilt parameters labelled (strike, dip). Annotate each to indicate the direction the V’s point and whether the V’s are wider or narrower than the topographic contours.

deliverables.label: Comparative analysis (250–350 words)
deliverables.description: Compare all three dip scenarios and address: (a) how outcrop band width changes as dip increases from 20° to 60° to 90°; (b) why vertical beds produce straight contacts regardless of topography; (c) how the V-pattern of tilted beds compares with the topographic V. Conclude with one sentence connecting dip angle data to a slope stability or groundwater context.

criteria.label: Screenshot set completeness
criteria.description: All three dip scenarios captured in map view; strike/dip labelled; V-direction and band width annotated on each.

criteria.label: Comparative analysis
criteria.description: Accurately explains band width trend, vertical bed behaviour, and V-pattern vs contour comparison; reasoning is geometric and clear.

criteria.label: Practical application
criteria.description: Practical conclusion is geologically sound and links a specific dip scenario to a real hazard or groundwater context.

assignments.attribution: Exercise design inspired by Abbey, A.L. (California State University, Long Beach). Hosted using Visible Geology (visiblegeology.com, Seequent Ltd.).

assignments.title: Strike, Downstream Dip, and the Rule of V’s
assignments.subtitle: Complete the Rule of V’s by testing downstream dipping beds and varying strike
assignments.description: Continuing from the previous assignment, use the same Visible Geology valley model to test two remaining dip scenarios: beds dipping downstream at 60° and beds dipping downstream at 20° (in Visible Geology, reverse the RHR dip direction to point dip downstream). Then rotate the strike while keeping dip constant and observe how the orientation of outcrop bands shifts. Delete previous Tilt events from the History panel before each new test. After all experiments, synthesise your observations into a complete written summary of the Rule of V’s — a foundational concept applied in every subsequent mapping assignment.
learningGoals: Distinguish map patterns produced by beds dipping upstream versus downstream at the same dip angle
Explain how dip angle affects V-pattern width when beds dip downstream at rates above and below the valley floor gradient
Describe how changing strike rotates the orientation of outcrop bands in map view
Articulate the complete Rule of V’s across all five bed orientations (horizontal, vertical, upstream, downstream steep, downstream shallow)

deliverables.label: Screenshot set — downstream dip scenarios
deliverables.description: Two 2D map-view screenshots: (1) beds dipping downstream at 60°, (2) beds dipping downstream at 20°. Label the dip direction and angle on each. Annotate which direction the V’s point and whether they are narrower or wider than the topographic contours.

deliverables.label: Strike variation screenshot and description
deliverables.description: One 2D map-view screenshot showing the beds tilted with a strike other than due North (any angle except 0° or 90°). In 2–3 sentences describe how the orientation of outcrop bands has changed compared to the north-striking model and explain why.

deliverables.label: Rule of V’s written summary
deliverables.description: Write a clear summary of the Rule of V’s addressed to a fellow geology student who has not completed this exercise. Cover all five bed orientations: (a) horizontal, (b) vertical, (c) dipping upstream, (d) dipping downstream more steeply than the valley floor, (e) dipping downstream less steeply than the valley floor. For each, state which direction the V points and whether the V is wider, narrower, or identical to the topographic V. This will be a reference you carry into the Lighthouse Bay and Three River Hills mapping assignments.

criteria.label: Downstream dip screenshots
criteria.description: Both downstream scenarios captured; dip direction and angle labelled; V-direction and relative width correctly annotated.

criteria.label: Strike variation description
criteria.description: Screenshot shows a non-north strike; description correctly identifies and explains the rotation of outcrop bands.

criteria.label: Rule of V’s completeness
criteria.description: All five orientation cases addressed; V-direction and V-width statements are correct for each.

criteria.label: Rule of V’s clarity
criteria.description: Summary is written clearly enough for a student unfamiliar with the concept to apply it; correct geological vocabulary throughout.

assignments.attribution: Exercise inspired by Abbey, A.L. (California State University, Long Beach), “How Geologic Beds and Other Planar Features Interact with Topography: Rule of V’s.” Hosted using Visible Geology (visiblegeology.com, Seequent Ltd.).

assignments.title: Geological Mapping — Lighthouse Bay
assignments.subtitle: Introductory full mapping exercise on a virtual coastal landscape
assignments.description: Lighthouse Bay is an entry-level virtual mapping landscape. Navigate the 3D environment, identify rock unit boundaries and structural features, plot your observations on the provided field slip, and produce a completed geological map with a cross section. Conclude with a brief geohazard commentary identifying any coastal or slope instability risks associated with the mapped geology.
learningGoals: Plot rock unit boundaries from virtual field observations onto a base map
Apply correct strike/dip symbols at observed outcrop locations
Construct a geological cross section A–B from a completed geological map
Identify and explain potential geohazards from the mapped geology

deliverables.label: Completed geological map
deliverables.description: Filled-in Lighthouse Bay field slip (no outcrops version) with all rock unit boundaries, strike/dip symbols, formation colours, a legend, north arrow, scale bar, and section line A–B. Submit as a PDF scan or photograph.

deliverables.label: Geological cross section A–B
deliverables.description: A cross section constructed perpendicular to the regional strike. Must include a topographic profile as the top of the section, all mapped units projected to depth, and correct dip angles.

deliverables.label: Geohazard commentary (150–200 words)
deliverables.description: Identify one geohazard relevant to the Lighthouse Bay geology (e.g., cliff instability, landslide susceptibility, coastal erosion) and explain the specific geological controls — including which rock units or structures are responsible.

criteria.label: Map accuracy
criteria.description: Unit boundaries, symbols, and colours correctly placed and internally consistent with virtual landscape observations.

criteria.label: Cross section quality
criteria.description: Section line clearly marked on map; topo profile accurate; units correctly projected below surface at consistent dip.

criteria.label: Geohazard identification and reasoning
criteria.description: Hazard is geologically plausible; specific geological controls are correctly explained.

criteria.label: Cartographic presentation
criteria.description: Map has north arrow, scale bar, legend, section line, and title.

assignments.attribution: Virtual landscape environment developed by the University of Leeds, School of Earth and Environment (see.leeds.ac.uk/virtual-landscapes). Exercise format adapted for this course.

assignments.title: Geological Mapping — Three River Hills
assignments.subtitle: Intermediate mapping exercise with varied strike, dip, and structural complexity
assignments.description: Three River Hills is the original Leeds Virtual Landscapes geological mapping exercise. The landscape contains multiple rock units with varied dip and strike. Map the geology, produce a cross section revealing the subsurface geometry, and write a structural analysis identifying any folds or unconformities visible in the map pattern. Conclude with a human-impacts note on how the structural geology could affect land use or infrastructure.
learningGoals: Map a multi-unit geology with varying strike and dip across a 3D landscape
Identify structural patterns (folds, unconformities) from map patterns
Construct a cross section that reveals subsurface geometry
Apply structural geology knowledge to human-impact and geohazard contexts

deliverables.label: Completed geological map
deliverables.description: Filled-in Three River Hills field slip with all unit boundaries, strike/dip symbols, formation colours, north arrow, scale bar, legend, and section line clearly marked.

deliverables.label: Geological cross section
deliverables.description: Cross section through the map area showing all mapped units at depth. Include a topographic profile. Add a brief caption explaining the subsurface geometry revealed by the section.

deliverables.label: Structural analysis (200–300 words)
deliverables.description: Describe the structural geology of Three River Hills: identify any folds, faults, or unconformities evident in the map pattern and explain what they reveal about the deformation history.

deliverables.label: Human-impacts note (100–150 words)
deliverables.description: Briefly describe how the structural geology could affect land use, infrastructure siting (roads, buildings), or natural hazard risk in the Three River Hills area. Reference specific map features.

criteria.label: Map accuracy
criteria.description: All boundaries and symbols are correct and internally consistent across the map.

criteria.label: Cross section
criteria.description: Section accurately portrays subsurface structure consistent with the map pattern.

criteria.label: Structural analysis
criteria.description: Correctly identifies structures present; deformation history interpretation is geologically reasonable.

criteria.label: Human impacts / hazard note
criteria.description: Demonstrates applied geology reasoning; specific features are referenced; risk assessment is credible.

assignments.title: Stereonets and Fold Map Patterns
assignments.subtitle: Explore how stereonets and geological map patterns relate to each other
assignments.description: Using the Visible Geology Geology Explorer and Stereonet tools (Blatchford, EMU), investigate how the map pattern of folded layers corresponds to equal-area stereographic projections of the same structural data. Work through the pre-loaded fold models to build stereonet construction and interpretation skills that are essential for the Rhoscolyn assignment and the CYOA project.
materials: Exploring relationships between map patterns of cylindrically folded layers and their stereonets.pdf
learningGoals: Plot planar and linear data on an equal-area lower-hemisphere stereonet
Construct a pi-diagram from fold limb bedding measurements
Derive fold axis plunge and trend from a stereonet pi-girdle
Articulate what aspects of fold geometry a stereonet cannot communicate

deliverables.label: Completed activity worksheet
deliverables.description: Work through all models in the activity PDF. For each model include: (a) a sketch of the relevant map-face pattern with strike/dip symbols; (b) a photograph or export of your constructed stereonet; (c) written answers to the interpretation questions in the activity.

deliverables.label: Synthesis paragraph (150–200 words)
deliverables.description: Summarise the key geometric relationship between a pi-girdle on a stereonet and the fold axis in 3D. Include one concrete example of how you would apply this to your Rhoscolyn dataset or to a structural project involving real field data.

criteria.label: Stereonet accuracy
criteria.description: Poles plotted at correct positions; pi-girdle drawn correctly; fold axis read accurately with correct plunge/trend.

criteria.label: Block face sketches
criteria.description: Map patterns correctly reproduced with appropriate structural symbols.

criteria.label: Synthesis and application
criteria.description: Accurately describes the geometric relationship; application example is geologically sound and specific.

assignments.attribution: Activity worksheet: Blatchford (Eastern Michigan University), “Exploring Relationships Between Map Patterns of Cylindrically Folded Layers and Their Stereonets.” Hosted on Visible Geology (visiblegeology.com, Seequent Ltd.).

assignments.title: Geological Mapping — Rhoscolyn
assignments.subtitle: Advanced mapping on a real complexly deformed coastal landscape
assignments.description: Rhoscolyn is a real location on Anglesey, Wales, with complexly deformed Precambrian metasediments. This is the most challenging Leeds mapping exercise. In addition to producing a geological map and cross section, you will construct a stereonet (pi-diagram) from your bedding measurements to analyse fold geometry. The assignment concludes with a coastal geohazard assessment evaluating how structural weaknesses contribute to cliff instability and landslide risk.
learningGoals: Map complexly deformed metasediments in a real virtual landscape
Construct and interpret an equal-area lower-hemisphere stereonet from bedding data
Derive fold axis orientation (plunge and trend) from a pi-diagram
Evaluate coastal geohazard risk informed by structural geology observations

deliverables.label: Completed geological map
deliverables.description: Filled-in Rhoscolyn field slip with all unit boundaries, structural symbols (strike/dip, fold axes, foliation if observed), legend, north arrow, and scale bar. Use the whole-area slip for context.

deliverables.label: Geological cross section
deliverables.description: A cross section through the mapped area showing folded units and any inferred faults. The section must be internally consistent with both your map and your stereonet analysis.

deliverables.label: Stereonet analysis
deliverables.description: A pi-diagram or beta-diagram constructed from your bedding measurements. Identify the fold axis orientation (plunge and trend) and classify the fold (upright / inclined / recumbent; plunging / non-plunging). Include the plotted stereonet as a figure.

deliverables.label: Coastal geohazard assessment (250–350 words)
deliverables.description: Assess the coastal geohazard risk at Rhoscolyn. Explain how the orientation of structural weaknesses (cleavage planes, fold limbs, inferred faults) relative to the coastal cliffs could contribute to rockfall or landslide. Suggest at least one practical mitigation measure and note any human infrastructure that could be at risk.

criteria.label: Map accuracy
criteria.description: Boundaries, unit patterns, and structural symbols are correct and consistent with outcrop observations.

criteria.label: Cross section
criteria.description: Correctly projects folded layers to depth; internally consistent with both the map and stereonet.

criteria.label: Stereonet quality and interpretation
criteria.description: Poles plotted at correct positions; pi-girdle drawn and interpreted correctly; fold axis read accurately; fold classified.

criteria.label: Geohazard assessment
criteria.description: Structurally informed; identifies specific failure mechanisms tied to mapped features; mitigation is appropriate and specific.

criteria.label: Cartographic presentation
criteria.description: All cartographic conventions followed; work is clearly labelled and well-organised.

assignments.title: Basin Stratigraphic Correlation
assignments.subtitle: Interpret sedimentary basin structure from geological maps, virtual drill cores, and subsurface models
assignments.description:
Oil and gas exploration has generated more than 150 years of subsurface data from North American sedimentary basins. In this three-part assignment you use those data — represented through geological maps and virtual drill cores — to investigate the Appalachian basin, then build your own subsurface model of the adjacent Illinois basin.

Part 1 — Appalachian basin map and model: Load the pre-built Visible Geology model below (Southern PA to SW OH transect, ~10× vertical exaggeration, actual dip ~5°). In both 2D map view and 3D block view, identify the western basin edge, the direction of regional dip, and how depth to Precambrian crystalline basement changes along the transect. Explain geometrically how these observations account for the concentric belts of progressively older surface bedrock seen on a geological map of the same area. Propose two alternative mechanisms — one involving subsidence, one involving uplift — that could produce the observed geometry.

Part 2 — Drill-core correlation: The model shows virtual cores at SW OH, Central OH, and Southern PA. Using these as constraints, sketch a predicted core for Northern WV (between Central OH and Southern PA). Show all geologic periods at appropriate relative thicknesses. Construct a colour-coded lithostratigraphic correlation diagram linking all four locations and explain why Pennsylvanian strata thickness varies across the transect.

Part 3 — Illinois basin model: Using the Visible Geology Geology Explorer, build a new block model of the Illinois basin. The Illinois basin contains the same Cambrian–Pennsylvanian stratigraphy as the Appalachian basin but has a circular, bowl-shaped outcrop pattern — youngest rocks at the centre, oldest at the margins. Set dip direction and magnitude to match this constraint. Add two virtual cores and correlate them, then propose a formation mechanism for this basin.
assignments.attribution: Adapted from Weislogel, A.L. (West Virginia University). “Basin Stratigraphic Correlation.” Visible Geology Activities Collection (visiblegeology.com). Appalachian basin model courtesy of Visible Geology / Seequent Ltd.
learningGoals: Relate the concentric surface bedrock age pattern of a sedimentary basin to regional dip direction and magnitude in the underlying strata
Apply the principle of lateral continuity to predict drill core stratigraphy at an unsampled location between two known cores
Construct a colour-coded lithostratigraphic correlation diagram across a basin transect and explain lateral thickness variations
Build a Visible Geology block model that honours geological map constraints for a new basin and add virtual drill cores to test subsurface predictions
Evaluate two competing mechanisms — regional subsidence versus flanking uplift — that could explain a sedimentary basin’s architecture

deliverables.label: Part 1 — Annotated model screenshots and written explanation
deliverables.description: Two annotated screenshots of the pre-loaded model: (a) 2D map view with the western basin boundary marked and an arrow showing dip direction; (b) 3D view with the crystalline basement visible. Accompany with a written explanation (200–250 words) of how regional dip, depth-to-basement change, and surface bedrock age pattern are geometrically related, and briefly describe two alternative mechanisms (subsidence vs. uplift) that could produce this geometry.

deliverables.label: Part 2 — Northern WV core prediction and lithostratigraphic correlation diagram
deliverables.description: A hand-drawn or digitally produced sketch of the predicted Northern WV drill core, placed in position between the Central OH and Southern PA cores. Include all geologic periods at appropriate relative thicknesses. Draw correlation lines connecting equivalent units across all four locations (SW OH → Central OH → Northern WV → Southern PA). Colour and label each geologic period. Add 100–150 words explaining why Pennsylvanian strata are thicker toward one end of the transect.

deliverables.label: Part 3 — Illinois basin model, cores, and formation hypothesis
deliverables.description: A Visible Geology block model of the Illinois basin with the same stratigraphic units as the Appalachian model. Dip direction and magnitude must honour the bowl-shaped, concentric outcrop pattern (youngest rocks at centre). Include two virtual cores — one in an area with Pennsylvanian strata, one without — and a correlation diagram. Provide a shareable model link and at least two screenshots (2D and 3D). Add a 250–350 word formation hypothesis addressing which sense of vertical motion is involved, why sediment accumulates at the basin centre, and what one additional data type (e.g., seismic profile, palaeontological record) could test your model.

criteria.label: Part 1 — basin map analysis and mechanism discussion
criteria.description: Basin boundary and dip direction correctly marked; basement visible in 3D view; written explanation accurately links dip, basement depth, and bedrock age pattern; two plausible mechanisms described.

criteria.label: Part 2 — core prediction and correlation diagram
criteria.description: Northern WV core unit sequence and relative thicknesses are geologically plausible; correlation diagram correctly connects all four sites; Pennsylvanian thickness variation is explained with specific geological reasoning.

criteria.label: Part 3 — Illinois basin model and cores
criteria.description: Model dip pattern matches the bowl-shaped Illinois basin map geometry; two cores positioned appropriately; correlation diagram produced; shareable link provided.

criteria.label: Part 4 — formation hypothesis
criteria.description: Mechanism is geologically valid; evidence from the model is explicitly cited; at least one specific, testable additional data type is identified.

assignments.title: Reservoir Geology and CO₂ Sequestration
assignments.subtitle: Construct stratigraphic columns, model lateral facies variability, and evaluate subsurface CO₂ storage sites
assignments.description:
Carbon capture and underground storage (CCS) is a key strategy for reducing atmospheric CO₂ from industrial point sources. In this three-part assignment you assess potential storage sites in the Upper Devonian Hampshire Formation of the Appalachian basin using real archived core descriptions, Visible Geology block models, and structural analysis.

Part 1 — Stratigraphic column construction: A detailed bed-by-bed description of a 30 ft Hampshire Formation core from Northern WV is provided in the assignment materials (Table 1). The core is divided into three stratigraphic units: Unit 1 (offshore shale/mudstone, 0–6.7 ft), Unit 2 (nearshore fine-grained sandstone, 6.7–18.05 ft), and Unit 3 (delta-plain coarse-grained sandstone, 18.05–30.05 ft). Using the blank log template and symbol legend in the assignment PDF, construct a formal sedimentary log. Identify whether the stacking pattern records overall shoreline transgression or regression.

Part 2 — Lateral facies modeling: The Hampshire Formation was deposited by a delta system prograding from eastern Pennsylvania westward toward Ohio. Build representative core models in Visible Geology for Central OH (distal) and Western MD (proximal). Adjust the proportion of each facies unit accordingly: Central OH should show a greater proportion of offshore mudstone; Western MD should include delta-plain or alluvial-plain units. Layer colours: offshore = grey, nearshore = light yellow, delta plain = dark orange, alluvial plain = green.

Part 3 — Structural trapping analysis: A thick mudstone overlies the Hampshire Formation, forming an impermeable seal. Modify your Central OH model (tilt 5° east, 2× vertical exaggeration) and Western MD model (fold: axis trend/plunge 022/10°, amplitude 16, wavelength 20, no vertical exaggeration). Annotate fluid migration directions on screenshots, then rank all three locations — Northern WV, Central OH, Western MD — for CO₂ storage viability and recommend one site.
assignments.attribution: Adapted from Weislogel, A.L. (West Virginia University). “Reservoir Sandstone Stratigraphic Correlation.” Visible Geology Activities Collection (visiblegeology.com). Hampshire Formation core description archived by the West Virginia Geological and Economic Survey.
learningGoals: Construct a formal stratigraphic column (sedimentary log) from a bed-by-bed core description table, applying the principle of superposition
Infer overall shoreline transgression or regression from the vertical stacking of offshore, nearshore, and delta-plain facies
Predict how the proportion of offshore, nearshore, and delta-plain facies varies along the axis of a prograding delta system
Build Visible Geology core models that reflect relative position along the delta progradation direction and justify the facies proportions chosen
Apply tilt and fold events in Visible Geology and interpret the resulting structural trap geometry for subsurface CO₂ migration
Rank multiple sites for CO₂ storage viability by integrating reservoir porosity, structural trap geometry, and seal integrity

deliverables.label: Part 1 — Hampshire Formation stratigraphic column and transgression/regression interpretation
deliverables.description: A completed sedimentary log for the Northern WV core using Table 1 from the materials. The column must include: the grain-size axis (clay → gravel), a depth scale (0–30 ft), the correct lithological symbol for each bed at proportional thickness, key sedimentary structures noted in the right-hand column, and the three stratigraphic units labelled with their depositional environments. Submit as a scan or digital file. Add 150–200 words identifying whether the overall stacking pattern records transgression or regression, with geological reasoning.

deliverables.label: Part 2 — Visible Geology core models (Central OH and Western MD)
deliverables.description: Two Visible Geology block models — one for Central OH, one for Western MD — each with at least one vertical core. Facies proportions must reflect the delta progradation direction (more offshore toward OH; more delta-plain/alluvial toward MD). Layer colours must match the standard legend. Provide one shareable link per model and a screenshot of each with the core visible. Add 50–75 words per model justifying your choice of facies proportions.

deliverables.label: Part 3 — Structural trapping analysis and CO₂ site ranking
deliverables.description: Modified models for Central OH (tilted 5° east, 2× VE) and Western MD (fold parameters as specified) with updated shareable links and screenshots annotated with arrows showing fluid migration direction through the reservoir. A ranked assessment (350–500 words) of all three locations for CO₂ storage viability, addressing: (a) reservoir rock quality, (b) structural trap geometry, and (c) seal integrity. Conclude with a specific recommendation for one location backed by geological evidence.

criteria.label: Stratigraphic column quality
criteria.description: Grain-size axis correct; depth scale accurate; all beds represented with correct lithological symbol at proportional thickness; three units labelled with environments; key structures noted; transgression/regression interpretation correct and justified.

criteria.label: Lateral facies models
criteria.description: Both models built with shareable links provided; facies proportions reflect delta progradation direction; colours match the legend; vertical cores added; proportions justified in writing.

criteria.label: CO₂ storage ranking and reasoning
criteria.description: Both models correctly modified with tilt/fold events; fluid migration annotated on screenshots; all three sites ranked; reasoning integrates reservoir quality, trap geometry, and seal integrity; recommendation is geologically justified.

assignments.title: Building a 3D Geological Model
assignments.subtitle: Synthesise your map and cross section into a Visible Geology 3D model
assignments.description: Using your completed Rhoscolyn map and cross section as input, construct a 3D geological model in the Visible Geology Geology Explorer. Apply deformation events (tilting, folding, faulting, erosion) in the correct sequence to reproduce the observed geology. Annotate screenshots for submission and write a geological history narrative that concludes with a note on whether any aspect of the geology poses a hazard or has been affected by human activity.
learningGoals: Translate 2D map and cross section data into a 3D digital geological model
Apply deformation events (tilt, fold, fault, erosion) in the correct geological sequence
Evaluate the internal consistency of a geological interpretation across 2D and 3D representations
Communicate geological structure and history in a clear written narrative

deliverables.label: Annotated 3D model screenshots (×3 minimum)
deliverables.description: At least three screenshots of your model: (1) plan/top view, (2) cross-section face matching your drawn section, (3) oblique 3D view. Each screenshot must be annotated with unit labels and key structural features (fold hinge, fault trace, etc.).

deliverables.label: Events history table
deliverables.description: A table or bulleted list of every event added to the model (e.g., 'Added 4 horizontal sedimentary layers', 'Tilted 35° NW', 'Tight anticlinal fold') with a brief justification for each, tied to evidence from your map or cross section.

deliverables.label: Geological history narrative (200–300 words)
deliverables.description: A chronological geological history of the field area as interpreted from your model, map, and cross section. Conclude with a brief note on whether the geology poses any hazard or has been affected by human activity in the area.

criteria.label: Model–map–section consistency
criteria.description: 3D model matches the map pattern and cross section; deformation sequence is geologically valid.

criteria.label: Screenshot annotations
criteria.description: All key features clearly labelled; views chosen effectively communicate 3D structure.

criteria.label: Geological history narrative
criteria.description: Events in correct chronological order; correct terminology used; hazard/human-impact note is geologically plausible.

criteria.label: Event justification
criteria.description: Each modelling choice is clearly tied to evidence from the map or cross section.

assignments.title: Independent Mapping Project — Proposal
assignments.subtitle: Design your own geology mapping project
assignments.description: Design and propose an original geological mapping project on a topic of your choosing. Projects may be conducted entirely online using remote-sensing data (satellite imagery, LiDAR, published maps) or in the field on public land (all risks assumed by the student). Every project must produce a geological map, a geological cross section, and a human-impacts or geohazard assessment. Structurally complex projects must also include a stereonet analysis. Submit your proposal as a PDF covering all eight required sections.
materials: Choose Your Own Adventure Final Mapping Project.pdf

locationOptions.label: Remote Structural Geology
locationOptions.description: Map folds, faults, or joints in a selected area using satellite imagery, Lidar from OpenTopography, and published datasets. Analyse structural data with a stereonet.
locationOptions.hazardTheme: Seismic hazard, slope stability assessment, or dam/reservoir siting

locationOptions.label: Remote Geomorphic / Quaternary Mapping
locationOptions.description: Map landslide deposits, glacial landforms, paleo-shorelines, river terraces, or alluvial fans using DEMs (e.g., OpenTopography) and satellite imagery.
locationOptions.hazardTheme: Landslide or flood hazard, coastal erosion, or infrastructure vulnerability

locationOptions.label: Remote Lithologic Mapping
locationOptions.description: Map rock unit boundaries using multispectral imagery (Sentinel-2, ASTER, Google Earth) and published geological maps. Validate against the published literature.
locationOptions.hazardTheme: Resource extraction impacts, groundwater contamination, or land subsidence

locationOptions.label: Field Structural Geology
locationOptions.description: Conduct field mapping of a structurally complex area on public land. Collect strike/dip measurements, plot on a field slip, construct a stereonet. All safety regulations apply; field work is entirely voluntary and all risks are assumed by the student.
locationOptions.hazardTheme: Rockfall hazard, slope stability, or fault proximity to infrastructure

locationOptions.label: Field Geomorphic / Engineering Geology
locationOptions.description: Map geomorphic hazards or engineering geology features (soil creep, erosion gullies, frost-heave terrain) at a local site on public land.
locationOptions.hazardTheme: Erosion, ground subsidence, or foundation conditions for structures

proposalSections.label: 1. Project summary
proposalSections.description: A brief overview of what you will map, where, and why it is geologically interesting.

proposalSections.label: 2. Location / study area
proposalSections.description: Describe the location; include coordinates or a map extract. If field-based, confirm the site is on public land.

proposalSections.label: 3. Hypothesis to be tested
proposalSections.description: A clear, testable geological hypothesis your map will address (e.g., 'The landslide deposits at X are controlled by the dip of underlying bedding').

proposalSections.label: 4. Type of data to be collected
proposalSections.description: Specify all data types: outcrop observations, strike/dip measurements, Lidar DEMs, satellite imagery, published maps, etc.

proposalSections.label: 5. Method of data collection
proposalSections.description: How will data be collected? Name specific tools (Google Earth Engine, OpenTopography, compass-clinometer, QGIS, etc.).

proposalSections.label: 6. Equipment list
proposalSections.description: List all required equipment. If field-based, include safety equipment (first-aid kit, communication device, etc.).

proposalSections.label: 7. Expected deliverables
proposalSections.description: List all outputs: geological map (type and scale), cross section, stereonet if applicable, hazard/impact assessment.

proposalSections.label: 8. Safety acknowledgement (field projects only)
proposalSections.description: If conducting any field work, confirm you have read the relevant field safety guide and understand that all risks are your responsibility.

deliverables.label: Proposal PDF covering all 8 sections
deliverables.description: A single PDF document covering all eight proposal sections listed above. Be concise but specific: a good proposal is typically 1–2 pages.

criteria.label: Project scope and feasibility
criteria.description: Project is achievable within the remaining camp timeframe; hypothesis is clear, specific, and testable.

criteria.label: Methodology and deliverables
criteria.description: Data collection methods are appropriate for the project type; all required deliverables are explicitly listed.

criteria.label: Hazard / human-impacts integration
criteria.description: A specific, relevant geohazard or human-impacts theme is explicitly incorporated into the project design.

assignments.attribution: Original assignment design for this virtual field camp course.

assignments.title: Independent Mapping Project — Final Submission
assignments.subtitle: Submit your completed self-designed geology mapping project
assignments.description: Submit your completed mapping project as a single PDF. All projects must include: a geological map (at the scale specified in your proposal), a geological cross section with topographic profile, and a human-impacts or geohazard assessment referencing specific map features. Projects with significant structural data must also include a stereonet analysis. Your PDF should contain all deliverables specified in your approved proposal.
materials: Choose Your Own Adventure Final Mapping Project.pdf

milestones.label: Stereonet complete (if required by project type)

deliverables.label: Completed geological map
deliverables.description: Your geological map at the scale specified in your proposal. Must include: legend, north arrow, scale bar, section line(s), and at least 5 structural symbols (strike/dip, fold axes, fault traces) where applicable to your project type.

deliverables.label: Geological cross section
deliverables.description: At least one cross section through your map area with a topographic profile and correctly projected units. Include a brief caption explaining what the section reveals about subsurface geometry.

deliverables.label: Stereonet analysis (required for structural projects)
deliverables.description: Required if your project is 'Remote Structural Geology' or 'Field Structural Geology'. Include plotted poles/planes, interpreted pi-girdle or best-fit great circles, fold axis orientation, and written fold classification.
deliverables.condition: Project type is remote-structural or field-structural

deliverables.label: Human-impacts / geohazard assessment (300–500 words)
deliverables.description: A written assessment integrating your mapping results with your chosen geohazard or human-impacts theme. Reference at least three specific features shown on your map. Suggest at least one mitigation or management recommendation.

deliverables.label: Supporting documentation
deliverables.description: Any supporting materials: field notes, GPS tracks, screenshots of remote-sensing tools, data sources, or references.

criteria.label: Map quality and accuracy
criteria.description: Unit boundaries are geologically consistent; structural symbols are correct; all cartographic conventions followed.

criteria.label: Cross section quality
criteria.description: Topographic profile is accurate; units project correctly to depth; section is consistent with the map.

criteria.label: Stereonet (structural projects only, otherwise pro-rated)
criteria.description: Poles and planes plotted correctly; fold axis interpreted accurately; fold classified with correct terminology.

criteria.label: Hazard / human-impacts assessment
criteria.description: Grounded in mapped geology; at least three specific map features referenced; recommendations are actionable and realistic.

criteria.label: Overall integration and geological reasoning
criteria.description: Map, section, stereonet, and narrative form a coherent, internally consistent geological interpretation.
